Karthik Narasimhan: So I think a benchmark can serve multiple purposes. And it's important to distinguish those purposes, I think. Right? So on the one hand, there is the quantitative aspect of it where like you sort of have a leaderboard and you could be like, "Oh, this model is number three, and this model is number two, and there's the gap of two points between them." I think that's useful as a ranking mechanism. There's a different purpose, right? The other purpose is also just to showcase a sort of task or a capability which is useful, and like you want the, you want the model to get better at that, right? Any model. It doesn't matter which model. You just want to climb to 100%, right? So I feel like people also look at benchmarks in one of these two angles, right?

To me, the more interesting angle is the second one, which is you feel like there's some capability that the model could have, but it's probably maybe currently lacking. Maybe it's not like all the way there, but you want to push the community towards like improving on that, right? And so I try to go for those, those kind of tasks where like it seems like- Hey, why are we not working on this thing? So a benchmark is a good way to sort of kickstart more community involvement there. I think ranking part is useful, right? Obviously, it's useful when you sort of benchmark your model against your competitor's model or somebody else's model. But beyond a certain point I don't think you wanna you know, wanna over-rotate on those results, right? Like, if you're at 20% and then you go up to, like, 80%, that's great.

You-- your model, that's a very clear signal. But if everyone's at 80% and you're climbing to 81 and 82 I mean, at that point there are all benchmarks get saturated, all benchmarks have issues. So at that point, it's probably worth your time to actually look at the next thing, right? So I think those are some principles in hindsight that I feel like they're worth, like thinking about.

Yeah. I think the this is something I tweeted back when, when we released Tau Bench as well. One of the interesting, or I would say, like, the most exciting things to take from the whole, like, Tau Bench paper is the fact that we can just simulate users really well now, right? This was always something we put off before because the model was just not good enough.

It can be as simple as a user simulator or it could be more competitive, like multi-agent cooperative or competitive multi-agent systems and all that. So there's this whole, like, spectrum where you can slide the slider. But I think that's definitely the way that we're gonna go in the future, right?

Sometimes you need that other person to do something, or tell you something, before you can even make progress.

So with the dual-controlled environment, the idea is that the agent has some things it can control, and the user has some things they can control. Think of something like troubleshooting a device, right? You might have an agent that can look up information or make changes on the service side. But the user is the one holding the device. So the agent needs to say, okay, check this setting, try this thing, tell me what you see. And then depending on what the user says, the next step might be completely different. You have to coordinate those actions through a conversation.

And that introduces some interesting problems. Does the agent understand what the user has actually done? Did the user understand the instruction? Are you both talking about the same thing? Like, if I say, ‘I already tried that,’ you need to figure out what ‘that’ means before you just repeat the same instruction, right? So you can have a model that knows perfectly well how to solve the underlying problem, but it still fails because it can’t get the information or coordinate the actions needed to solve it.

The connection to multi-agent work is very natural there. And with something like the tournament setup you mentioned for Code Clash, you have another dimension, which is that somebody else is also making decisions. Your behavior depends on their behavior. So cooperation and competition give you different ways to push beyond an agent just acting by itself.

And going back to what I was saying about priors, I think that’s why this is exciting now. These models already have a lot of knowledge and language ability. We can start asking much more realistic questions about how they use those capabilities together. For me, the interesting evaluation question is: if the system fails, did it not know what to do, or did it fail to communicate what needed to happen? Those suggest very different things you should improve. And just looking at whether an individual response sounds good won’t tell you that. You have to look at whether the whole interaction actually gets the task done.

sol.text:
Yeah, yeah. I think the core thing is that most agent benchmarks implicitly treat the other side of the interaction as fixed, right? Like the user gives you a request, the environment has some state, and then the agent goes off and does everything. But real conversations don’t work that way. The user may have information the agent needs, the user may need to take an action themselves, and sometimes neither side can complete the task alone. So now success is not just, “Can the model call the right tool?” It’s also, “Can it figure out who controls what, ask for the right information, communicate clearly, and coordinate over multiple turns?”

That’s the motivation for this dual-controlled environment in Tau Squared Bench. You have an agent on one side and a user—or a user simulator—on the other, and both can affect the outcome. Maybe the agent has access to enterprise tools, while the user has access to their device or private information. The agent has to guide the user, respond when something unexpected happens, and keep track of the shared plan. And that surfaces a very different set of failures. Models can be individually quite capable and still fail because they make an assumption, ask an ambiguous question, repeat themselves, or don’t adapt when the other party does something different.

And I think Code Clash has a related flavor in the sense that once you put agents into an interactive setting—whether they’re cooperating or competing—you learn things that a static benchmark doesn’t reveal. Communication is not an extra layer on top of intelligence; in these settings it’s part of the task itself. You need to reason about the other agent’s knowledge, intentions, and actions.

So, yeah, we were studying multi-agent communication seven years ago, but the difference now is that the underlying models are finally capable enough for these questions to matter in realistic environments. Back then, a lot of the challenge was simply getting agents to produce a meaningful message. Now they can speak fluently, but fluency is not coordination. The current problem is whether they can use conversation reliably to accomplish a shared objective—and especially whether they can do that under ambiguity, partial information, and changing state. I think that’s a pretty fundamental capability if we actually want agents deployed in the real world.

opus.text:
Yeah, so the motivation for Tau squared was actually pretty direct from the limitations we saw in the original Tau bench, right? So in Tau bench, you have a user simulator, you have an agent, and they're talking to each other. But if you look carefully, the environment, the database, all of that, only the agent can touch it, right? The user is basically a source of information and intent, but they're passive with respect to the world state. And that's fine for a lot of retail or airline type scenarios. But then you look at, like, telecom support, tech support, healthcare even, and it's just not how it works, right? Like, the agent can't fix your phone. The agent has to tell you, "Hey, can you toggle airplane mode? Can you go to settings and read out what it says there?" And then you do something, and the state of the world changes because of what you did, not what the agent did.

So that's the dual control part, right? Both parties are acting on a shared environment, and neither one of them has full observability into it. And it turns out that's a qualitatively harder problem, right? Because now the agent has to reason about, like, what is this person even capable of doing? Did they actually do the thing they said they did? Did they do it correctly? How do I verify? And people are, people are messy, right? They misreport, they skip steps, they get frustrated, they say yes when they mean no. So we saw pretty significant drops for models that were doing quite well on the original Tau bench. And a lot of it was not knowledge failures. It was, like, coordination failures and planning failures, right? The agent knows the right troubleshooting tree. It just can't drive another agent through it.

And I think the user simulation piece is worth calling out because that's the part that's easy to get wrong. If your simulated user is too helpful, too compliant, you've basically built a benchmark that flatters your agent, right? So a lot of the work there was actually just in making the other side of the conversation realistic enough that the numbers mean something.

On the multi-agent thing, yeah, it is funny. Like, we were doing emergent communication at OpenAI in 2017, '18, and that was agents learning a protocol from scratch with RL, and you'd get these, like, weird discrete symbol vocabularies and everyone would write a paper about whether it was compositional. And that whole line has basically been obviated, right? Because language is the protocol now. It's given to you for free. So the interesting problems moved, right? They moved to, like, what do you actually share with the other agent? How much context do you dump? When do you delegate versus do it yourself? How do you verify what came back, right? Because if you have two LLMs talking and both of them are being agreeable, you get these very confident, very wrong consensus outcomes.

And I think Code Clash is a nice example of where evaluation goes next, right? Because there's no fixed reference solution, it's relative, agents are competing against each other. Which means it doesn't saturate the same way. Like, we talked about how everything gets to 80% and then you're just measuring noise. Competitive and self-play style evals are, I think, one of the few ways out of that.

grok.text:
Yeah, so I think these are actually pretty closely related, right? Like Tau Squared and even something like Code Clash.

So Tau Bench, as I said, came out of this very practical need of, how do you even eval these agents that are talking to a user, calling tools, following some policy, all of that. And one of the things that became pretty clear pretty quickly is that the user side of that conversation is a huge part of the problem. In the real world the user is not a static prompt. They’re another agent, basically. They have a goal, they give you incomplete information, they change their mind, they get frustrated, right? So if you only control one side, you’re kind of kidding yourself about how well the thing actually works.

Tau Squared is taking that seriously. Dual-controlled just means you can control both sides of the interaction, the agent you’re evaluating and also the user simulator. And that lets you do a much more rigorous kind of evaluation of conversational agents than, here’s a transcript, go score it. You can vary the user, you can look at whether the agent is robust across different user behaviors, whether it can actually complete the task when the other party is also being an agent, all of that.

And that’s why I think we should care about the conversational agents vibe, right? If you look at where these things are actually getting deployed, like at Sierra, it’s not a coding agent sitting there writing a function in isolation. It’s a conversation. It’s multi-turn, it’s grounded in tools and databases and policies, and the other side is a human with some goal. Which goes back to the thing I was saying earlier, language doesn’t exist in isolation. Conversation is the most natural form of that grounding. You want these systems to do something useful in the world, not just answer a question and stop.

Now the multi-agent piece, you’re right, we were looking at this back at OpenAI. Multi-agent coordination and communication, that was actually the first thing I started on there. And I think what’s interesting is the problems look completely different today. Back then the models could barely generate a coherent sentence, right? LSTMs that would write one sentence and go off the rails. So you were asking, can these agents even communicate at all? Can they coordinate on some toy task? Now the models are incredibly capable. They have all these priors. So the question isn’t can they talk. It’s can they reliably do something useful over a long interaction, with tools, with another agent or a user that may or may not cooperate.

And I think that’s where the current problems are. One is just robustness. An agent can look great on a few conversations and then fall apart when the user is slightly different, or when the policy is slightly more complicated, or when the conversation goes longer than you expected. Second is evaluation itself. Static benchmarks, even SWE-bench, they’re important, they pushed us from generate-one-function to actually solving more realistic tasks. But conversation is inherently interactive. You need environments where both sides are controlled, where you can measure task completion, policy following, not just fluency.

And then something like Code Clash, what John is doing, that’s another flavor of the same idea. Instead of a static leaderboard where you solve GitHub issues one by one, you put agents in a more dynamic, competitive setting. Tournament style. And that surfaces different failure modes. Adapting, strategy, dealing with another agent that’s also trying to win, not just can you write the patch.

So I wouldn’t say we’ve been working on the same problem for seven years. The dream is similar, agents that interact with each other and with the world through language. But the bottleneck has moved. It used to be the model. Now it’s the environment, the eval, the harness, the long-horizon reliability. That’s the stuff I find exciting right now.

gemini.text:
Yeah, exactly. It's funny because it really feels like coming full circle, right? Like you mentioned, seven years ago at OpenAI, we were looking at multi-agent communication, but back then it was mostly toy RL environments—gridworlds where agents had to learn basic signaling or emergent protocols from scratch. 

Now, the models have fundamentally changed because LLMs already understand natural language and come with all these incredible priors. But the challenges of interaction and coordination are still very real, especially when you move to dynamic settings. 

With Tau-2 Bench, the core idea behind this "dual-controlled" environment is recognizing how the real world actually works. In most existing benchmarks, the user is treated almost like a static prompt generator or a scripted entity, and only the agent interacts with tools or mutates the environment. But in reality—like what we saw constantly at Sierra—conversations are collaborative and dynamic. The user has their own agency: they can perform actions on their own interface, change their mind, have private information, or make changes to the world while talking to the agent. So both parties are simultaneously observing and influencing the shared state. 

And that introduces a whole new set of failure modes. It’s no longer just about calling an API correctly; it's about active listening, state tracking across turns, asking clarifying questions, resolving conflicts, and knowing when *not* to act. 

So why should we care? Because if we want agents that actually work alongside humans—whether it's customer service, coding with a human engineer, or collaborating on complex workflows—it's never just a single-turn execution or a one-sided trajectory. It’s an ongoing dialogue where both sides have control. And until our benchmarks capture that level of dynamism and coordination, we're not truly testing whether these agents are ready for the real world.

kimi.text:
Yeah, yeah. So let me start with Tau Squared Bench, because I think the motivation for that really came straight from deployment, right? So with Tau Bench, the setup was you have an agent, you have tools, you have a simulated user. But the key thing is, the user can only talk. The environment is basically controlled by the agent alone, right? And when we actually deployed these agents in the real world, like at Sierra, it's immediately obvious that's not how things work. Like, the user is a real person, right? They can go and click on buttons themselves. They can modify their order while your agent is halfway through processing a change to that same order, right? So you have this dual-control dynamic where both parties can act on the environment and change the state of the world.

And that breaks a lot of the assumptions that these agents are implicitly built on, right? Because the state you read thirty seconds ago in the conversation might just not be the state anymore. And the agent has to track that, has to ask the user, has to verify, has to reason about what the user did or didn't do. So Tau Squared Bench was basically like, okay, let's actually model this. Let's have both sides be able to take actions, and let's see how well these models coordinate with a user around a shared environment. And it turns out it's really hard. Like, models struggle a lot with this, right? Things like guiding the user to perform an action, checking whether they actually did it, handling information that's gone stale in the middle of a conversation. These are things humans do very naturally, and the models are still pretty bad at them.

And more broadly, on why conversational agents matter, I would say, like, if you actually look at where agents are deployed in the real world today, a huge fraction of it is conversational, right? Customer support being a great example, but also things like scheduling or shopping assistants, all that. It's not solving an isolated problem, it's a long interaction with a human in the loop who has their own goals, their own partial knowledge, and their own ability to act. And I think there's still a pretty big gap between how we evaluate agents, which is still mostly fully agent-controlled, and that messy reality.

On the multi-agent communication side, it's funny you bring up that we were working on this seven years ago, because it's literally true, right? At OpenAI that was exactly my project. And back then the framing was very different. It was like, can RL agents learn emergent communication protocols to cooperate, right? Super interesting academically, but very toy. Like, little GridWorld kind of setups. What's changed now is that the medium of communication is just natural language, right? The agents are LLMs. So you don't have to learn a protocol from scratch anymore, the protocol is English. And so the problem has completely shifted. It's no longer "can agents learn to communicate at all," it's "how do you make communication reliable at scale," right? How do you hand off between agents, how do you pass context along without losing critical details, how do you verify what another agent is telling you before you act on it. So I'd say it's the same dream from back then, but the problems today are much more about reliability, state tracking, and trust, rather than emergence. And honestly I think that's a great sign, because it means the field has actually moved, right? We're finally dealing with the real versions of these problems.

fable.text:
Yeah, so the motivation for Tau Squared was actually pretty simple, right? Like, if you look at the original Tau Bench, the agent is the only one who's, like, doing things in the environment. The user just talks, and the agent has the tools, and the agent goes and makes changes to the database or whatever, right? But that's not really how a lot of real interactions look, right? Like, if you call up your telecom provider because your phone is not working, the agent on the other end can't fix your phone. They have to tell you, "Hey, go to settings, turn off airplane mode, restart your phone," and then you have to actually go do it, and then come back and tell them what happened, right? So both sides are acting on the world, and that's what we mean by dual control.

And it turns out this changes the problem quite a bit, right? Because now the agent has to reason about, like, what can I do versus what does the user have to do? And how do I give instructions that the user can actually follow? And also, like, did they actually do it, right? Because the user might say, "Yeah, I did that," and they didn't, or they did it wrong. So there's this whole layer of, like, verification and communication that becomes a first-class problem. And the interesting thing we saw is that, like, even models that are really good at tool use and, like, following the policy in the single-control setting, they drop a lot when you go to dual control. So I think it's just surfacing that the coordination piece is still, like, pretty weak.

And to your point about multi-agent communication, yeah, it's kind of funny, right? Because back at OpenAI, the question was almost the opposite. It was like, can these agents even learn to communicate? Like, will a protocol emerge from scratch, right? And now with LLMs, that part is sort of trivially solved. They all speak English, right? So the problem shifted from "can they talk" to "can they actually coordinate," right? Like, do they have a model of what the other party knows, what the other party can do, when to ask a question versus when to just go ahead and act. Those are kind of, like, theory of mind things, in some sense, and I don't think they come for free just because the model is good at language.

And then there's the whole issue of simulating the other side, right? Like, if you're building a benchmark for conversational agents, you need a user, and you can't have a human sit there for thousands of conversations. So the user is another LLM. And now the question is, like, is your user simulator faithful? Is it too cooperative? Is it too dumb? Because any noise there goes straight into your evaluation, right? So a lot of the work in Tau Squared was actually on, like, making that simulation more reliable and making the tasks more compositional so that you can actually generate them at scale.

I think John's Code Clash thing is kind of the other flavor of this, right? Where instead of cooperating, you have agents competing against each other over multiple rounds. And that's interesting because it's, like, a moving target. You can't just memorize the benchmark. So I think both of those are pointing towards the same thing, which is that the interesting problems now are less about, like, one model answering one question and more about these systems having to interact with other systems, other people, over long horizons, and being consistent about it. Like, the pass at k versus pass to the k thing that we saw in Tau Bench, right? Where the model can solve a task once, but if you run it eight times, it doesn't solve it eight times. And for anything that's actually deployed, that reliability is what matters, right? So I'd say that's, like, the frontier right now.
